title: His first cracked clarinet and the kazoo
summary: His father paid eight or nine dollars for a cracked clarinet that was hard to blow; he never used a fife.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: I'm not trying to pry into your personal affairs. How much did you pay about when you first got it?
I paid about, I think my father paid about eight or nine dollars for it.
Yeah, some kind of thing is an opportunity for that.

I didn't know that in the case. Even today you could. Yeah, and it was through this particular friend of mine, this fellow by the name of Alfred Gishaw, he told me that the instrument wasn't no burden. I thought it was all right, you know, and they had about two cracks in it, one at the top and one at the bottom. Did it leak pretty bad?
Did it get hard to blow?

Well it was very hard to blow, very hard. And being in the Albert system too and just learning how to play and trying to make one particular note which would be natural was supposed to be the hardest note to make on it because you had to stretch so, you know. And I found it very difficult at first, but I later got adjusted to it. But it wasn't until later until I found out what the real reason was.
So had you ever played a little kin fife or anything like some of the kids do to learn your fingering first?
It was just kazoo. Did you finger the kazoo any or just sing it?
Well they had three holes in it, but there wasn't too much control with it. The only tonal control I would say would be from the top if you held your hand on the top and raised it up from—
